Status: accepted

## Context

A node that keeps local state on its data disks — a persistent volume, an image
cache, a database — keeps that state on hardware that eventually leaves the
building: an RMA, a decommission, a rack in a colo somebody else has keys to.
[Issue 6](https://github.com/Corium-OS/Corium/issues/6) asked for a way to
declare disk encryption from the `corium:` block rather than hand-writing
`cryptsetup` into cloud-init.

The request splits the same way software RAID and ZFS did, and the split is the
whole decision.

**Data disks.** Extra disks to be encrypted, formatted and mounted. This can be
done at first boot, and it is what this ADR adds.

**The root filesystem.** By the time the `corium:` block is read, root is
deployed, mounted, and running the process reading it. An encrypted root must
additionally be unlocked in the initramfs, before anything Corium ships has
started. Out of scope, for the same reasons a RAID root
([ADR 3](/docs/decisions/adr-0003-software-raid-scope/)) and a ZFS root
([ADR 7](/docs/decisions/adr-0007-zfs-data-disks/)) are.

Unlike ZFS, this costs the image nothing: `cryptsetup`, `systemd-cryptenroll`,
the crypttab generator and `tpm2-tss` are all already in `fedora-bootc`. There
is no variant image and no new package.

## Decision

`luks[]` covers data disks. Volumes are created by `corium-agent` at first boot,
before k0s is installed, on the same footing as `raid[]` and `zfs[]`. Each
volume names a device, how it is unlocked, and optionally a filesystem and a
mount point.

Two unlock methods, exactly one per volume:

- **`tpm2`** (the default) seals the key to the machine's TPM with
  `systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=auto`.
- **`passphrase`** takes a passphrase, inline or — as everywhere else in the
  schema — resolved through a `SecretSource` at first boot.

There is no fallback chain. A volume with two ways in has the weaker of the two
as its real security, and nothing in the configuration says which that is.

Ordering is `raid[]`, then `zfs[]`, then `luks[]`, all before k0s. That makes a
volume on top of a `/dev/md/<name>` legal and useful — redundant storage that is
also encrypted — and a pool on top of a volume impossible, which is a smaller
promise than the alternative and an honest one. A device claimed by any one of
the three fields may not be claimed by another; that is checked at validation,
before anything touches a disk.

## Why TPM is the default

The alternative default is a passphrase, and a passphrase means one of two
things on a server. Either somebody types it at the console on every boot — so
the node does not come back from a power cut until a human walks to the rack,
which is not a property anyone wants in a Kubernetes node — or it is stored on
the machine, which is the key-file case below.

TPM sealing gives the unattended boot without storing a key anybody can read:
the volume opens on this machine and on no other. On hardware with no TPM the
enrolment fails loudly at first boot, which is the correct outcome for a node
that asked for encryption it cannot have.

## What the key file does and does not protect against

Be plain about this, because "encryption at rest" is a phrase that invites
people to assume more than they bought.

A `passphrase` volume's key is written to `/etc/luks-keys/<name>.key`, mode
`0600`, in a `0700` directory, so later boots are unattended. `/etc` is on an
unencrypted root. So:

- **A disk that leaves the machine is protected.** Pull the data disk, plug it
  into anything else, and it is ciphertext. That covers the RMA, the
  decommission, and the drive that walks out of a colo — which is the threat
  most nodes actually face.
- **A machine that leaves the building is not.** The key is on the root disk,
  next to the volume it opens. Anyone with the whole machine has both.
- **A running node is not.** The volume is mounted; anything with root on the
  node reads it as plain files. LUKS protects data at rest, not from the OS
  that mounted it.

**`tpm2` has the same shape, reached more elegantly.** The key is in the TPM
rather than in a file, so it cannot be copied off; but the TPM will unseal for
whoever boots the machine, so a stolen machine is still a stolen machine. Unless
the volume is enrolled against PCRs and the boot chain is measured and Secure
Boot is on — a chain Corium does not configure and should not pretend to — TPM
unlock is protection against a stolen *disk*, exactly like the key file.

The honest summary is that both methods buy the same thing. `tpm2` buys it
without leaving a readable key on disk, which is why it is the default;
`passphrase` buys it on hardware with no TPM, and on a disk an operator may need
to open somewhere else. Neither is protection against an attacker with the
running machine, and the documentation says so where an operator will read it.

## Why this earns its place over cloud-init

cloud-init has no notion of encryption: its `disk_setup` partitions and formats,
and `cryptsetup` would have to go in `runcmd`. That recipe gets three things
wrong.

- **Ordering.** A `runcmd` races the kubelet. Lose the race and containerd
  writes into the directory on the *root* disk that the volume is then mounted
  over — invisible afterwards, still consuming root. Corium unlocks, formats and
  mounts before k0s, and writes a `RequiresMountsFor` drop-in so Kubernetes
  refuses to start rather than run without its storage.
- **Refusing to destroy data, and refusing harder than RAID does.** A device
  already carrying a filesystem or a partition table stops the bootstrap unless
  `wipe: true`, as for `raid[]`. A device already carrying a **LUKS header is
  adopted and unlocked, never reformatted**, whatever `wipe` says:
  `cryptsetup luksFormat` replaces the header in place, and the old header held
  the only copy of the key for everything behind it. There is no undo and no
  consent flag that should make that convenient.
- **The passphrase is a secret.** Written into `runcmd` it sits in cleartext
  instance metadata, readable by anything that reaches the metadata service —
  which leaves the encryption protecting nothing. `passphraseFrom` resolves it
  through the same path as a join token.

## Consequences

**A TPM-sealed volume is readable on exactly one machine.** That is the feature
and the risk. Clear the TPM, replace the mainboard, or lose the node, and the
data is gone — there is no recovery key, because a recovery key that Corium
generated would have to be shown somewhere, and the only somewhere available at
first boot is the journal. A data disk is not a backup; this makes that truer
than usual.

**The temporary key never reaches a disk.** A TPM volume has to be formatted
with *some* key before the TPM slot can be enrolled. Corium generates 32 random
bytes, writes them to `/run` (a tmpfs), formats, and enrols with
`--wipe-slot=password`, which removes that slot only once the TPM slot is in
place. An interrupted enrolment leaves a volume that can still be opened rather
than one that cannot.

**Unlocking goes through crypttab, not directly through cryptsetup.** The entry
that will open the volume on every future boot is the entry that opens it now,
so a crypttab line that would have failed at the next reboot fails at first boot
instead — while an operator is watching, and before k0s has put anything on the
disk.

**Nothing is added to the image.** Everything needed is in `fedora-bootc`
already.

## Alternatives considered

**Clevis and `clevis-luks-askpass`.** The other common TPM-unlock path, and the
one Fedora documents for network-bound unlock (Tang). Rejected: it is a package
to add, a second unlock mechanism beside the one systemd already ships, and its
real advantage — Tang, unlock bound to a network service — is a piece of
infrastructure Corium would then have to have an opinion about. If network-bound
unlock is ever wanted, this is the decision to revisit.

**Encrypting the root filesystem.** Rejected for the reasons above: the decision
is made at install time, by the installer, before `corium-agent` exists. A node
that needs an encrypted root is installed that way, with the installer's own
support for it. Corium goes further than declining to do it — it refuses a
device the running system has mounted, so pointing `luks[].device` at the booted
disk fails rather than destroying the machine.

**A recovery key enrolled alongside the TPM.** `systemd-cryptenroll
--recovery-key` prints one. Rejected because there is nowhere safe to print it:
first boot's only output is the journal, and a recovery key in the journal is a
recovery key in the log aggregator. An operator who wants one can enrol it by
hand afterwards, which is a documented step and a deliberate act.

**A fallback from TPM to passphrase.** Rejected: see above. Two ways in means
the security of the weaker one, silently.

**Document a `cryptsetup` recipe and add no field.** Rejected for the reason
ADR 3 rejected it for RAID and ADR 7 for ZFS: it leaves the ordering problem
unsolved, and the ordering problem is the one that quietly corrupts a node.
